1.11.2 ▶

1.1 — Launch: Fork, Clone & Press Play

Today you get the world you will bring to life over the next four months. The sprites are drawn, the tilemaps are laid out, and your character is already breathing an idle animation. But press Play and try to move: nothing happens. That is not a bug you are hunting — it is the whole point. Every script in this project is an empty shell, and you are going to fill them in yourself by reading Unity's documentation, breaking big problems into smaller ones, and building one mechanic at a time.

Setup Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — Fork the starter. Log into GitHub, open the cs-curriculum-main repo your teacher links in Canvas, and click Fork (top right). A fork is a copy of the repo that belongs to you — your commits go to your copy, and you can never break the original.

Fork vs. clone — say it out loud: fork copies the repo on GitHub (server to server, yours forever). Clone downloads a repo to this machine (server to laptop). You do both today: fork first, then clone your fork.

Step 2 — Clone your fork. On your fork's page click the green Code button, copy the HTTPS URL, then in GitHub Desktop: File → Clone Repository → URL tab → paste → Clone. Or in a terminal: 

git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/cs-curriculum-main.git

Step 3 — Open it in Unity. Open Unity Hub → Add → pick your cloned cs-curriculum-main folder. The first open takes a while: Unity imports every sprite and audio file in the project. When it finishes, find Assets/_Scenes in the Project window. There are three scenes, and they are already wired to load one another: Start, Overworld, and Platformer.

Step 4 — Press Play. Open the Overworld scene and press the Play button at the top of the editor. Watch your character in the middle of the screen.

Tinker: A world with no code in it

  1. What is your character doing the moment Play mode starts? Does the sprite sit frozen, or is an animation playing? Describe exactly what you see.
  2. Press W, A, S, D, and the arrow keys. Does the character move across the grass at all?
  3. Look at the turrets on the map. Do they rotate, notice you, or fire anything? What does that tell you about the difference between graphics and gameplay?
  4. There is exactly one coin on this map. If the character cannot move, why can that coin not be collected yet?
Tour ~10 min

What is actually in this repo? Find each of these in the Project window, and read the third column carefully — it tells you what is really there:

FolderWhat lives thereCurrent state
Assets/_Scenes Start, Overworld, Platformer Three built scenes, already wired to load each other
Assets/Scripts PlayerController, EnemyController, TurretController, Projectile, StatManager, Lever Every one is an empty shell — a class with blank methods. Nothing runs.
Assets/Prefabs Player, Coin, Spikes, MobileEnemy, Turret, Turret_Projectile, AxeItem, Switch Pictures with tags. No physics, no behaviour.
Assets/Artwork Top-down grass and stone tiles, cave tilesets, characters, weapons All the art is finished and ready to use
Assets/Animations The coin's spin animation Already playing — the coin is the one thing that looks alive
Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts CameraController, SceneSwitch, TopDown_EnemyAnimator The only working code you inherit. The camera follows you and the caves load — that is it.

Why so empty? Because reading a finished game and nodding along teaches you almost nothing. Instead, this year you take real game behaviours — collecting a coin, taking damage, aiming a turret, jumping — and break each one into small answerable questions:

  • What Unity event fires when two shapes touch? (You will read OnTriggerEnter2D)
  • How is a harmful spike different from a friendly coin? (Triggers versus collisions)
  • What maths finds the distance from a turret to its target? (You will read Vector3.Distance)

Socratic

  1. Your character already plays an idle animation without a single line of your code. Who or what is driving that animation right now?
  2. Why is building a game system yourself from documentation more useful for learning computer science than reading a finished project and answering questions about what each line does?
Ship It ~10 min

Commit — the habit that starts today. In GitHub Desktop (or git add / git commit -m / git push), commit with the message "1.1: cloned the starter" and push. From now on, every single class ends with a commit and a push. Your commit history is the proof of your progress — and in June you will read it back to see how far you came.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain the difference between a fork and a clone
  • Open the Overworld scene in Unity and enter Play mode
  • Say what your character does on Play, and confirm it cannot move yet
  • Name the three scenes and find Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs in the Project window
  • Commit and push your work to your own GitHub repository
